title: Kernel path telemetry and LLM fallback bench
summary: SE-led deep dive to share kernel-level telemetry approach, discuss nondeterministic CUDA-graph signals, evaluate TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs for our on-prem VPC footprint, and agree pilot benchmarks plus security docs. Customer concerned about tail latency, KV cache eviction across restarts, and SSO/KMS integration.
action_items: Samir Patel: share kernel-level telemetry dashboard link and CSV by 2025-10-03
Jules Ortega: run targeted p95/p99 bench on 8k sequence workload and upload results to shared sheet by 2025-10-06
Carlos Rios: provide sample network topology and firewall rules for on-prem VPC by 2025-10-02
Priya Kaur: send SSO/SAML and KMS compliance questions by 2025-10-05
next_steps: Schedule 2-hr pilot kickoff for v1 benchmark (TensorRT-LLM on prem vs vLLM on dedicated) week of 2025-10-13
Exchange benchmark artifacts and baseline payloads (shared by Redwood)
Redwood to provide security package and SOC2 report link
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Ortega (Redwood SE), Nina Zhou (Redwood SE), Logan Reed (Redwood Product), Maya Lin (Aurelia Head of ML), Carlos Rios (Aurelia Infra), Priya Kaur (Aurelia Security), Ethan Browne (Aurelia SRE)

Optional auto sections:
Summary: see metadata field above.
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/bench/aurelia-kernel-report (redwood internal bench sheet), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (security packet)

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining on a monday, appreciate the time. quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: hi maya here, head of ml at aurelia. we're trying to stabilize inference for clinical summarization - lots of long sequences, p95 spikes are killing UX.
[00:16] Carlos: carlos infra, we run in a hybrid VPC - some on prem racks connected via express link, NVLink across nodes for model shards in the future.
[00:24] Priya: priya security, i'll be validating SAML, KMS integration and data residency needs.
[00:30] Samir: great, our SE jules will lead runtime/bench details. jules over to you.
[00:36] Jules: thanks. i'll try to keep it pragmatic - goal today is to show how we collect kernel path telemetry, what signals indicate cuda-graph nondeterminism and eviction, and then what that means for trt-llm versus vllm for your load.
[00:48] Jules: quick baseline question - what's your typical seq len distribution? average? tail?
[00:54] Maya: we're doing a lot of 2k to 8k sequences, median around 1.6k but 10% are > 4k, the clinical notes especially. we also have concurrent real-time summaries with bursts of smaller requests.
[01:10] Jules: perfect, that explains the tail. vLLM's async scheduler and kv cache behavior tends to be different with long KV chains compared to tensorrt-llm which aggressively fuses kernels and relies on cuda-graphs for stable performance.
[01:25] Ethan: quick interjection: our ops worry is eviction - if a node restarts or we OOM we need kv persistence, otherwise warmup kills p95.
[01:34] Nina: yep, that's where persistent KV and prefetch strategies come in. Redwood's runtime supports both in-memory and optional persistent store for prefix caches. we can snapshot the KV to disk or an NFS during low-traffic windows.
[01:46] Carlos: NFS is noisy, we'd prefer a block-store attach or our in-cluster Ceph. any perf hit?
[01:53] Jules: there is overhead; our telemetry shows a 4-8% increase in p50 but reduces cold-start p95 by up to 60% for your workload shape when the KV hit rate is high. i'll share the raw CSVs.
[02:08] [02:08] Samir: walk us through the kernel telemetry - what are you collecting?
[02:12] Jules: we collect per-invocation kernel IDs, launch duration, cudaGraph replay counts, memory alloc/free events, and a lightweight timeline that marks when the runtime chooses trt kernels vs aten/torch fallback. we also capture nvtx ranges so you can correlate with model layers.
[02:30] Carlos: sometimes our tracing names get munged, does your telemetry preserve function-level mapping to model op?
[02:36] Jules: mostly yes but there are fuzzy spots - the symbolization step can mislabel custom fused ops; we include heuristic mapping and you can upload your local model build for better mapping.
[02:46] Maya: we've seen nondeterministic behavior with cuda-graphs where repeated inputs sometimes cause a different kernel selection mid-sequence, causing small latency spikes - is that expected?
[02:56] Jules: welcome question. it's usually from execution path divergence: when quantized kernels have guard conditions or when the runtime switches between cached cudagraph and dynamic execution due to memory fragmentation or unexpected sequence length. small changes in batch composition cause different kernel fusion decisions.
[03:12] Nina: and that shows up as a 'signalized path change' in our telemetry - a sudden swap from trt kernel X to aten fallback, with accompanying increase in latency.
[03:22] [03:22] Maya: does tenstro.. trt-llm handle those falls back gracefully? we don't want output variance.
[03:27] Jules: trt-llm is typically faster for highly batched stable shapes, but its fused kernels and cuda-graph reliance make it more brittle to dynamic shapes; vLLM's more dynamic exec path gives more stable tail latencies in mixed workloads, but often at a throughput cost.
[03:45] Samir: high level tradeoff is throughput vs tail stability + determinism.
[03:49] Ethan: can you quantify? p95 numbers?
[03:52] Jules: from our internal bench on a 48GB A100-ish node with your seq distribution: trt-llm can reach ~450 tok/s at median with p50 ~12ms per token, p95 ~220ms for 4k seqs under moderate concurrency; vLLM median 320 tok/s p50 ~18ms, p95 ~140ms — so vllm had a better tail in that run but lower peak throughput. caveat: these are sensitive to quantization and batch strategy.
[04:28] Carlos: interesting, so vLLM better for our p95 but trt-llm gives better throughput if we can shape requests. what about mixed-quant setups?
[04:35] Jules: mixed-quant can complicate kernel selection. int8 paths often have specialized kernels that are not always available across all layers. our runtime can route specific layers to fp16 kernels while others run int8; telemetry shows that that mixed path adds about 5-15% variance in kernel launch times.
[04:57] Maya: we use conservative quantization right now because of accuracy sensitivity in clinical text. is there an incremental quantization strategy?
[05:03] Nina: yes, model-aware quant profiles: first pass we quant the feed-forward layers and keep attn in fp16, validate against held-out clinical prompts. we recommend running a small eval set to capture regen/semantic drift. we can automate that in Redwood Optimize.
[05:19] [05:19] Priya: security question - if KV is persisted to disk, how is that encrypted and who owns keys?
[05:25] Samir: we integrate with customer KMS, HSM support on Private deploys. you retain key ownership, Redwood only stores encrypted blobs. we'll send the key management whitepaper.
[05:33] Priya: and for VPC/on-prem the traffic doesn't leave the customer network?
[05:37] Logan: Private deploy means control plane can be hosted or customer-managed; data plane stays in your VPC with optional egress controls. we'll share the architecture diagram.
[05:47] [05:47] Maya: back to cuda-graphs - is there a way to make cudagraph replays deterministic when sequence lengths vary?
[05:52] Jules: two levers: 1) pad-to-fixed shapes and use dynamic masking (costly in memory but stabilizes graphs), 2) maintain multiple prebuilt graphs keyed by shape bins and route requests to the closest bin. Redwood can auto-bin shapes based on observed distribution.
[06:10] Carlos: does your binning increase memory pressure?
[06:13] Jules: yes, more graphs means more memory for the graph's workspace and potentially more persistent allocations. our telemetry records graph_counts, workspace_bytes, and eviction events so you can tune a tradeoff curve.
[06:24] Maya: can kernel telemetry be exported to our observability stack?
[06:27] Jules: absolutely — we can stream a subset of metrics to Prometheus and ship histograms to your existing Grafana. we also attach the nvtx spans so you can slice by model layer.
[06:36] [06:36] Ethan: any gotchas with NVLink and multi-GPU? we plan a shard strategy for embedding models.
[06:41] Nina: NVLink is great for large-shard models but watch out for fragmentation and cross-gpu cuda-graph reproducibility; our runtime prefers local kernels and falls back to inter-node comms which shows up as increased inter-GPU memcpy kernel events in telemetry.
[06:55] Jules: in practice we saw a 10-12% p95 penalty when a single token required cross-gpu KV fetch versus local KV in a multi-gpu setup.
[07:06] [07:06] Maya: talking about fallback heuristics - what policy drives choosing aten fallback vs trt kernel?
[07:11] Jules: it's a small decision tree: shape compatibility, precision match, workspace availability, and whether a cudagraph is cached. When any guard fails we fallback to aten or a blended kernel; telemetry logs the guard that tripped.
[07:24] Samir: do you keep a history of guard flips per session so we can correlate user sessions to kernel instability?
[07:28] Jules: yes, session-level path signals exist and we can aggregate by user_id/request_id. we anonymize by default.
[07:37] [07:37] Maya: what's the recommended pilot to prove p95 improvements?
[07:40] Jules: run a 48-hour pilot across the following: 1) baseline capture with your current infra (we'll collect traces), 2) TRT-LLM build with stable binning + aggressive cudagraphs, 3) vLLM build with async scheduler and persistent KV. Compare p50/p95/p99, cold-start behavior, and throughput.
[07:58] Carlos: how invasive is trt-llm integration? we run custom ops in our tokenization path.
[08:03] Nina: trt-llm requires model conversion steps and a build pipeline; custom ops need shim layers. vLLM can run more of your existing PyTorch graph with fewer changes. we'll help with conversion scripts.
[08:13] [08:13] Ethan: about observability, can we set alerts on 'kernel flip rate'?
[08:17] Jules: yes, we surface a 'path flip' metric (flips per minute) and recommend thresholds; above a small threshold we trigger fallback to a safer model variant or a CPU-hosted fallback to preserve availability.
[08:31] Maya: CPU fallback — that sounds expensive. what is the behavior?
[08:35] Jules: it's a last-resort: we spin a small CPU replica that serves a strict latency SLAs or returns a degraded response (shorter summary). it's about graceful degradation not long-term cost optimization.
[08:46] [08:46] Samir: demo time — Jules, can you share a quick telemetry trace?
[08:49] Jules: sharing screen now. (brief silence, screen flicker)
[09:00] [09:00] Jules: okay you can see a run from our internal bench: the left pane shows per-kernel durations (bars), middle shows graph_replay_count, right shows path flip markers. note at 00:34:12 there's a flip when the runtime decided to replay a different cudagraph due to fragmentation.
[09:21] Maya: that flip correlated with a 180ms spike in p95.
[09:25] Jules: exactly. we then manually forced binning and replayed the run — spike disappeared, throughput held.
[09:33] Carlos: can we auto-fix when a flip trend is detected?
[09:36] Jules: yes, Redwood can automatically expand a bin or fall back to a prebuilt safe graph. the tradeoff is memory. our recommended policy is conservative growth with alerting.
[09:48] [09:48] Priya: security again: when you auto-upload graphs or artifacts to redwood, are those sanitized?
[09:53] Samir: we only request hashes/metadata by default; artifacts can be uploaded to your S3 with a short-lived link if you want to keep ownership. we'll provide a signed upload flow.
[09:59] Maya: good. next, let's define acceptance criteria for pilot. p95 under 200ms for 4k sequences under X concurrency?
[10:05] Jules: propose p95 < 200ms for 4k seqs at a concurrency of 8 and throughput >= 300 tok/s sustained as a starting target. we can tune after initial run.
[10:17] [10:17] Ethan: what about cost estimates for dedicated on-prem nodes versus hosted?
[10:21] Logan: dedicated will look like a fixed reserved cost plus support; on-prem private has an upfront license and integration. we'll send detailed pricing after we size the pilot.
[10:31] Maya: do you have any examples of customers who moved from trt-heavy config to mixed vllm for tail reduction?
[10:36] Jules: yes, a genomics customer switched to hybrid: trt for batched offline jobs, vllm for real-time clinician queries. that reduced support tickets by 40%.
[10:45] [10:45] Carlos: about benchmark seeds - what payloads will you use?
[10:48] Jules: we'll use a stratified sample of your historical requests, anonymized. please share a 24-hour sample including token counts and timestamps; we'll provide a scraping script.
[10:58] Maya: i'll get that to you.
[11:01] [11:01] Samir: wrapping — can we recap action items and ownership?
[11:05] Samir: jules you'll run the targeted p95/p99 bench and share; samir will share telemetry dashboard; carlos provides network topology; priya security questions; maya will share sample requests. timeline 1-2 weeks.
[11:20] [11:20] Maya: thanks everyone, this was helpful. looking forward to the pilot.
[11:24] Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and links.

End of transcript.
